title: Not All Jokes Are Created Equal: Teacher Humor That Helps (and Hurts) https://www.learningandthebrain.com/blog/not-all-jokes-are-created-equal-teacher-humor-that-works/
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson (Learning and the Brain) reports on a German study that isolated the effects of different humour styles in a geography classroom by producing five otherwise-identical 17-minute videos on plastic ocean waste, each varying only in the teacher's use of humour: on-topic (funny cartoons about the content), off-topic (jokes about everyday life), self-deprecating, aggressive/student-deprecating, and no humour. Over 500 teachers and students rated the videos on teacher quality, interest, clarity, and time-on-task, with students also rating intrinsic interest and emotions. On-topic humour modestly improved ratings of teacher-student relationships and lesson interest and boosted students' self-reported intrinsic motivation while lowering negative emotions, with no cost to perceived clarity or time-on-task. Aggressive humour, by contrast, damaged teacher-student relationships, reduced motivation, increased anxiety and anger, and even made students feel the lesson was less clear and more time-wasted. Off-topic and self-deprecating humour had little measurable effect either way. Watson is careful to flag the study's real limits — it measured self-reported perceptions rather than actual learning, used one cultural context (Germany), and relied on a 17-minute video rather than an ongoing relationship with a real teacher — before landing on a simple, practical takeaway for teachers who are naturally funny.
points: The study's clean design isolates humour type as the only variable across five otherwise identical 17-minute lesson videos, letting researchers attribute rating differences specifically to on-topic vs. off-topic vs. self-deprecating vs. aggressive humour.

On-topic humour modestly improved perceived teacher-student relationships, lesson interest, and student intrinsic motivation, and lowered negative emotions — with no measured cost to clarity or time-on-task.

Aggressive/student-deprecating humour damaged relationships, motivation, and emotional state, and even made students perceive the lesson as less clear and more time-wasted, despite no actual change in content delivery.

Watson flags that the study measured self-reported perceptions, not actual learning outcomes, so the practical takeaway (use on-topic humour, avoid mocking students) is a plausible but unproven inference about downstream achievement.
Off-topic humour and self-deprecating humour had little measurable effect on any outcome — a useful null result against the common assumption that 'any' humour helps.
quotes: A research team in Germany made five videos, about 17 minutes long, for a geography class. In each video, the teacher covered the same content: plastic waste in the sea.

More specifically: on-topic humor got higher ratings for enhancing the teacher's relationships with the students, and resulted in lessons being rated as more interesting. Students who saw the on-topic humor video rated themselves as more intrinsically motivated, and gave lower ratings to the negative emotions (anger, anxiety, boredom).

Aggressive humor — are you shocked? — interferes with teacher/student relationships, reduces intrinsic motivation, and ramps up anxiety and anger. I myself was a little surprised to read that it lowers the students' rating of the lesson's clarity, and gives students the sense that they spent less time on task (although they didn't).
First: this study did not measure the effect of humor on LEARNING. The researchers did not measure how much the students learned as a result of different kinds of humor.

Third: humor depends A LOT on cultural expectations. I don't know much about the intersection of 'Germany,' 'humor,' and 'school culture.' But I know enough to wonder how well that Venn diagram aligns with other Venn diagrams in other cultures and countries.

If you're a funny person, you can use this study as a guideline. Don't mock your students; you knew that anyway. Don't waste time with jokes about Saturday Night Live; they're not having the effect you hope they do.
